instruction: Independently review every assigned ID in full scenario context; examine the first finding and any changed question. A pass on changed content also rechecks the repair. Do not edit the bank.

originalQuestion.prompt: If Gold1 blocks the upper side, what should you check next?
originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 changed the open-side cue. A new lane or a clear pass to Navy2 may fit, but the current space decides.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which two things help you carry with your head up?
originalQuestion.explanation: Pressure and support can both move. Checking Gold1 and Navy2 keeps the carry connected to what is open now.

originalQuestion.prompt: Place YOU in a lower open lane away from Gold1.
originalQuestion.explanation: This example leaves the upper pressure and keeps YOU moving in a separate lane. Other clear space may work.

originalQuestion.prompt: Why is moving and looking better than racing into Gold1?
originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 is in the straight path. Moving toward visible space while checking Navy2 can preserve puck control and a next choice.

originalQuestion.prompt: If Gold1 turns toward the middle, what should YOU protect first?

options.text: The space toward the navy end

originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 still has the puck and the navy end is the area at risk. Keep that space in view while supporting Navy2.

originalQuestion.prompt: Which two clues help YOU choose a recovery lane?

options.text: A fixed position from before the turnover

originalQuestion.explanation: The carrier and teammate positions change where help is useful. An old fixed spot cannot decide the new lane.

originalQuestion.prompt: Place YOU closer to the navy end while keeping Gold1 in front.
originalQuestion.explanation: This example recovers toward the protected end and keeps the carrier visible. Another lane may fit the moving play.

originalQuestion.prompt: What does “our job changed” mean here?
originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 has the puck, so Navy players must help defend. YOU should turn back, watch the carrier, and use Navy2's position to choose support.

originalQuestion.prompt: If Gold1 follows you, what should you look for?

options.text: A new clear angle to Navy2
The same spot even after Gold1 moves

originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 changed the first support spot. A new angle can help Navy2 if it stays visible and separate.

originalQuestion.prompt: What two details shape your support near the net?

options.text: A promise that the pass will arrive

originalQuestion.explanation: The carrier and defender define which support space is useful. A pass remains a possibility, not a promise.

originalQuestion.prompt: Place YOU on the lower side with Navy2 in view.
originalQuestion.explanation: This example separates YOU from the crowded net-side line and keeps the carrier visible. Another clear angle can work.

originalQuestion.prompt: Why should support move when the defender moves?
originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 can take away the first lane. Moving with the new picture gives Navy2 a better chance to see a safe option.

originalQuestion.prompt: If Gold1 closes the middle after your reception, what can you check?
originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 changed the middle. Navy3 or open ice may give YOU another choice if the lane is clear.

originalQuestion.prompt: What two facts describe this new play?
originalQuestion.explanation: The briefing says YOU received the puck, and Gold1 is pressure ahead. Navy2 is no longer the owner.

originalQuestion.prompt: Place YOU lower and to the side with Navy3 visible.
originalQuestion.explanation: This gives YOU another view of Navy3 while keeping Gold1 in front. It is one example support position.

originalQuestion.prompt: Why can Navy3 matter after Navy2 passes?
originalQuestion.explanation: Navy3 is a visible teammate on the lower side. After receiving, YOU can use that support if Gold1 closes the middle.

originalQuestion.prompt: Who has the puck now?
originalQuestion.explanation: The puck is loose, so nobody owns it yet. Find it before planning the next touch.

originalQuestion.prompt: What should you notice as you go to the puck?

options.text: A goal that has already happened

originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 is pressure near the approach, and Navy2 is a possible support player. Looking at both keeps the next touch connected to the play.

originalQuestion.prompt: Place YOU near the loose puck, with room to see Gold1.
originalQuestion.explanation: This spot brings YOU near the puck while leaving a little view of Gold1. It is one controlled approach example; another nearby spot can work.

originalQuestion.prompt: Put this puck pickup read in order.
originalQuestion.explanation: First find the puck, then notice the nearby players, then choose the next action. Looking while approaching keeps the read current.

originalQuestion.prompt: Gold1 gets closer while you approach. What is a good update?

options.text: Keep the puck on the far side and look again
Reach without checking because Navy2 is open

originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 is now more of a pressure cue. Protecting the puck away from pressure and looking again may keep Navy2 available; it does not promise a clean play.

originalQuestion.prompt: Why does Navy2 matter after you find the puck?
originalQuestion.explanation: Navy2 is a navy teammate in open middle space. After you see the pressure, that space can give you a short passing choice if the lane stays clear.

originalQuestion.prompt: If Gold1 closes YOU before the pass, what can Navy2 do?

options.text: Find Navy3 or another clear lane
Treat the planned pass as safe

originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 changed the planned reception lane. Navy3 or another clear choice can fit if the carrier can see it.

originalQuestion.prompt: What two facts say the pass is still only planned?
originalQuestion.explanation: Navy2 remains the owner and the reception has not happened. The planned pass can change with pressure.

originalQuestion.prompt: Place YOU lower and away from Gold1, still visible to Navy2.
originalQuestion.explanation: This example creates a new reception angle and separation from Gold1. Another clear target may work.

originalQuestion.prompt: Why should YOU keep moving before the pass arrives?
originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 is close and can take away the first lane. Moving to a clear angle gives Navy2 a current target instead of a fixed one.

originalQuestion.prompt: If Gold1 closes the lower outlet, what could Navy2 use?
originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 changed the lower outlet. Navy3 or another side may help if the carrier can see the lane.

originalQuestion.prompt: What two players shape the breakout choice?
originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1's pressure and Navy3's higher location give Navy2 two real cues for the next outlet.

originalQuestion.prompt: Place YOU a little inside the lower outlet, clear of Gold1.
originalQuestion.explanation: This example offers a lower-side target while keeping YOU separate from Gold1. Another clear outlet may work.

originalQuestion.prompt: Why can an outlet help without being the answer every time?
originalQuestion.explanation: A lower outlet can give Navy2 a different angle away from Gold1. If Gold1 closes it, Navy3 or another safe choice may be better.

originalQuestion.prompt: If Gold1 collects the blocked puck, what should YOU do first?

options.text: Read the new carrier and protect the navy end
Keep waiting for the old pass

originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 becoming the owner changes the role picture. Read the carrier and protected space before choosing a response.

originalQuestion.prompt: What two clues show the pass failed?
originalQuestion.explanation: The puck is loose and Gold1 touched the pass. YOU are not the owner in this freeze.

originalQuestion.prompt: Place YOU below the loose puck with Gold1 visible.
originalQuestion.explanation: This changes YOU's approach line while keeping the defender in view. It is one controlled recovery example.

originalQuestion.prompt: Why cannot YOU treat a blocked pass like a reception?
originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 touched the pass and the puck is loose. Ownership, pressure, and Navy3 must be checked before the next touch.

originalQuestion.prompt: If Gold1 turns away from Navy3, what should YOU keep?

options.text: The carrier and the navy end in view

originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1's turn changes the route, but the carrier and protected end remain the key defensive cues.

originalQuestion.prompt: What two facts make this a new defensive read?

options.text: YOU still have the old attack

originalQuestion.explanation: Gold1 owns the puck and Navy lost it. The roles changed with that event.

originalQuestion.prompt: Place YOU between Gold1 and the navy end, with Navy3 in view.
originalQuestion.explanation: This example recovers toward the protected end and keeps support visible. Another route can work.

originalQuestion.prompt: How can Navy3 help YOU choose a recovery lane?
originalQuestion.explanation: Navy3 shows where another navy player is, so YOU can avoid chasing the same space. Keep Gold1 and the navy end as the main cues.

manifest.riskReason: The follow-up is tied to a named goalie-freeze/retreat routine; local format and official instruction determine the action.

originalQuestion.prompt: If the goalie whistle ends the play, what should YOU check before moving?

options.text: The new puck owner and the coach's next instruction
A shot that was never shown

originalQuestion.explanation: A whistle changes the activity state. Check who controls the puck and what the coach asks before choosing a new place.

originalQuestion.prompt: What two details matter after the puck is tipped wide?

options.text: The old route no matter what

originalQuestion.explanation: The tip changes the puck location and may change the useful support. Both need a fresh look after the whistle or tip.

manifest.riskReason: The follow-up is tied to a named goalie-freeze/retreat routine; local format and official instruction determine the action.

originalQuestion.prompt: Place YOU a little away from the crease area with the puck side visible.
originalQuestion.explanation: This example gives YOU room after the named whistle while keeping the puck side in view. The coach's setup still controls the next move.

manifest.riskReason: The follow-up is tied to a named goalie-freeze/retreat routine; local format and official instruction determine the action.

originalQuestion.prompt: Why should a whistle make you reset your read?
originalQuestion.explanation: The puck may be in a new place and a different player may control the next action. Resetting prevents carrying an old plan into a changed activity.

findings.issue: The assigned follow-ups name Gold1, but this setup has no away skater for that named opponent.
findings.evidence: The scenario has only YOU and H2; actorDisplayName makes H2 read as Navy2, but there is no A1/Gold1 actor to block the upper side or occupy the lane.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact setup patch: add one away skater labeled A1 (displayed as Gold1) at a clearly supported upper-side position, then check each reference relationship and rehash q7–q10. If the scene is intended to remain two-player, rewrite all Gold1 prompts/options/explanations to use only the visible players.

findings.issue: The assigned follow-ups name Gold1, but this setup has no away skater for that named opponent.
findings.evidence: The setup has only YOU and H2; q7–q10 ask about Gold1 turning, blocking, or staying in front.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact setup patch: add one away skater labeled A1 (displayed as Gold1) at a coherent middle/goalward position and verify the circle relationship, then rehash q7–q10; otherwise rewrite those prompts to remove Gold1.

findings.issue: The assigned follow-ups name Gold1, but this setup has no away skater for that named opponent.
findings.evidence: The setup has only YOU and H2; q7–q10 ask about Gold1 following, moving, and defending near the net.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact setup patch: add one away skater labeled A1 (displayed as Gold1) at a scene-supported pressure position and verify q7–q10 against it, then rehash; otherwise rewrite the extension to use only visible actors.

findings.issue: Navy3 is named in assigned follow-ups but is absent from the setup.
findings.evidence: The setup contains YOU, H2 (displayed Navy2), and A1 (displayed Gold1); q7, q9, and q10 require a visible Navy3 support player.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact setup patch: add a home skater with a distinct ID and label H3 (displayed as Navy3) at the lower-side support position used by q9, then recheck q7/q9/q10 and rehash. Do not leave the child choosing an unseen player.

findings.issue: q7 offers Navy3 even though the loose-corner scene contains no Navy3.
findings.evidence: The setup has YOU, H2 (Navy2), and A1 (Gold1); there is no H3/Navy3 actor.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact setup patch: add a positioned H3 actor displayed as Navy3 only if the scene is rewritten to include that support option; otherwise remove Navy3 from q7 and use the visible Navy2/space choices.

findings.issue: Navy3 is named in q7 and q8 but is absent from the moving-back scene.
findings.evidence: The setup has YOU, H2 (Navy2), and A1 (Gold1); no H3/Navy3 is represented near the blue line.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact setup patch: add a home H3 actor displayed as Navy3 near the described blue-line outlet and verify the position prompt q9, or rewrite q7/q8 to use only Navy2 and the visible lower outlet.

findings.issue: q10 asks the child to check Navy3 although no Navy3 is present.
findings.evidence: The setup includes YOU, H2 (Navy2), A1 (Gold1), and A2 (Gold2); the briefing says Navy2 remains available but never introduces Navy3.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact setup patch: replace Navy3 in q10 with Navy2, or add a positioned H3/Navy3 and update the briefing; rehash q10 after the repair.

findings.issue: Navy3 is named in the assigned defensive follow-ups but is absent from the change-signal setup.
findings.evidence: The setup has YOU, H2 (Navy2), and A1 (Gold1); no Navy3 exists, and the briefing does not describe a Navy3 defensive state.
findings.recommendedChange: Exact setup patch: if retaining a defensive extension, add H3 displayed as Navy3 and state its position in the briefing; otherwise rewrite q7/q9/q10 around the actual change-signal scene and rehash.

findings.issue: The brief calls the loose puck near the side boards, but the puck is in the middle band.
findings.evidence: The puck is loose at y=-3 while rink side boards are at approximately y=±12.954; q2–q6 carry the incorrect board-side framing.
findings.recommendedChange: Rewrite the brief as a middle-lane approach, or move the puck/actors to a genuinely board-side setup. If keeping coordinates, replace q2–q6 board language with middle-lane/approach-angle language and rehash changed rows.

findings.issue: q5 tells the child to keep the puck on the far side before anyone owns it.
findings.evidence: The setup puck has owner null and the briefing calls it loose; the answer presumes successful control during the approach.
findings.recommendedChange: Replace q5 with: Gold1 gets closer while you approach the loose puck. What is a good update? Options: (a) Stay between Gold1 and the puck while you close under control; (b) Reach through Gold1 without looking; (c) Pretend the puck is already yours. Answer [a]. Explanation: The puck is still loose, so protect the approach and check Gold1 until you actually control it. Rehash q5.

findings.issue: The assigned follow-ups switch a loose-corner-puck freeze into a planned Navy2-to-YOU pass and invent a later reception.
findings.evidence: The current setup is owner:null at (26.5,8.5); the briefing says YOU are nearest, Gold1 approaches, Navy2 waits along the boards, and the approach is stated rather than simulated. No planned pass exists.
findings.recommendedChange: Replace q7 with: If Gold1 reaches the loose puck before YOU, what should you check? Options: (a) Who controls it and where Navy2 is; (b) Keep approaching as if it is yours; (c) Pass to Navy2 without looking. Answer [a]. Replace q8 with: What two facts describe this freeze? Options: (a) The puck is loose in the corner; (b) YOU are nearest it; (c) Navy2 already owns it. Answer [a,b]. Replace q9 with: Place YOU near the loose puck with Gold1 visible. Replace q10 with: Why should YOU keep checking before touching the loose puck? Explanation: Gold1 is approaching and nobody owns it yet, so update pressure and support before the next touch. Rehash changed rows.

findings.issue: q8 and q10 say Gold1 touched the deflected puck, but the current scene only says Gold1 is nearby.
findings.evidence: The briefing says the pass was deflected, the puck is loose, YOU have not collected it, and Gold1 is nearby. No Gold1 touch is stated; Navy3 is also absent for q10.
findings.recommendedChange: Replace q8 with: What two clues show the pass is not a reception? Options: (a) The puck is loose; (b) YOU have not collected it; (c) YOU already control it. Answer [a,b]. Replace q10 with: Why cannot YOU treat a blocked pass like a reception? Explanation: The puck is loose and YOU have not collected it. Check Gold1 and Navy2 before the next touch. Rehash changed rows.

findings.issue: q7–q10 describe a Gold1/Navy3 turnover that is absent from the current change-signal scene, and q8 marks that invented state as a scene fact.
findings.evidence: The briefing says the designated change signal has just sounded while YOU controls the puck; setup owner is home-skater-1 and no Navy3 is present. Gold1 collecting the puck is never stated.
findings.recommendedChange: Rewrite the extension around the stated change: q7 asks what YOU do after the signal; q8 asks for the two current facts (signal sounded and YOU controls the puck); q9 moves YOU only toward a represented exit/next-unit area; q10 asks why the coach signal must be followed. Keep the named half-ice rule scoped to this briefing and rehash changed rows.

findings.issue: q8 introduces a puck tipped wide that is not part of the goalie-freeze restart state.
findings.evidence: The briefing says the goalie already held the puck, the whistle happened, and Gold1 now controls the restart puck near the crease. No tip or wide puck is stated.
findings.recommendedChange: Replace q8 with: What two details matter before resuming? Options: (a) Gold1 has the restart puck; (b) The official's restart instruction; (c) The old attack continues unchanged. Answer [a,b]. Explanation: The whistle changed the activity state, so identify the current owner and follow the stated restart instruction. Rehash q8.

scenarios.title: A puck with nobody holding it
scenarios.objective: Tell a loose puck from a carried puck.
scenarios.briefing: The coach placed a puck in a quiet practice area. Nobody controls it yet. Navy2 waits beside the area. YOU are invited to collect it. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The puck is separate from both players.
Navy2 is waiting.
YOU are invited to collect.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck right now?
questions.explanation: The setup has no puck owner. It is between the players.

questions.prompt: What did the coach ask YOU to do?
questions.explanation: That is the instruction in the briefing.

questions.prompt: Arrange a gentle collection try.
questions.explanation: This is a suggested practice sequence; the picture does not measure skating or control.

questions.prompt: Show a place near the puck to finish your approach.
questions.explanation: The reference approaches without going far beyond the puck. Several nearby places may suit the activity.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 reaches it first and controls it. Is it still loose?
questions.explanation: The answer follows the stated new ownership event.

questions.prompt: How could you tell the puck was waiting for someone?
questions.explanation: Point to the separate puck and notice that neither player controls it.

questions.prompt: After YOU collect it, Navy2 asks for a pass. What helps before sending it?

options.text: Look to see if Navy2 is ready
Pass at once because you heard a call
Keep looking only at your stick

questions.explanation: A call helps you find Navy2. Look up and check that your partner is ready before passing.

questions.prompt: After the pickup, what helps a pass reach Navy2?

options.text: Aim where Navy2 stood before moving

questions.explanation: Find the partner and their ready stick. If Navy2 moves, the old spot may no longer be a useful target.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 to give YOU a short pass after the pickup. Leave room between you.
questions.explanation: This brings Navy2 onto a shorter passing line from the pickup area. A different clear target can work if both players are ready.

questions.prompt: You touched the puck, but it slid away. Is your pickup finished? Tell a grown-up.
questions.explanation: Touching the puck once is different from controlling it. Find it again, approach under control, and keep it close enough for your next touch.

scenarios.title: From the boards to the circle
scenarios.objective: Use boards and faceoff circle to understand a practice instruction.
scenarios.briefing: YOU are near the side boards. The coach names the nearby red ring a faceoff circle and asks you to return to its middle for the next turn. Navy2 waits outside the circle. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The boards are near YOU.
The named circle is centred near x=20.7, y=6.7.
Navy2 waits outside the circle.

questions.prompt: What does the coach call the nearby red ring?
questions.explanation: The briefing names this painted ring. It is a landmark in this practice.

questions.prompt: Where are YOU starting?
questions.explanation: YOU are close to the side boundary, outside the circle centre.

questions.prompt: Arrange the return to our practice spot.

options.text: Check that the space is clear

questions.explanation: This is a suggested activity reset, not a faceoff rule or skating test.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the middle of that faceoff circle.
questions.explanation: The reference is the stated practice spot. The coach could accept a nearby clear place; no tactical optimality is claimed.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 stands in the middle first. What could you do?
questions.explanation: Give your partner room and follow the coach's next instruction.

questions.prompt: Point to the boards, then point to the circle.
questions.explanation: Recognizing the two named areas is the aim. A point or spoken answer is enough.

questions.prompt: It is Navy2’s turn in the circle. Where could YOU wait?

options.text: At the middle spot beside Navy2

questions.explanation: Let your partner use the practice space. Wait in a clear place outside and listen for your turn.

questions.prompt: Before leaving the boards for your turn, what should YOU check?

options.text: Where the coach asked you to go
Whether the way there is clear
Whether you can beat Navy2 to the spot

questions.explanation: Find the named practice spot and check your route. Getting there first is not the aim of this reset.

questions.prompt: For another waiting spot, move Navy2 outside the circle on its centre-ice side.
questions.explanation: This waiting spot stays outside the painted circle and gives the next player room. The coach can choose another clear waiting place.

questions.prompt: Can you skate across the painted circle line to reach the middle? What should you look for?
questions.explanation: The circle is paint on the ice, not a wall. You can cross it in this activity after checking the way is clear and it is your turn.

scenarios.title: Listen for the practice stop
scenarios.objective: Recognize a stated practice stop signal.
scenarios.briefing: In this practice only, one whistle means stop under control and listen. It has just sounded. YOU hold the puck; Navy2 uses a separate lane. This is not a match restart rule. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: A practice stop signal was stated.
YOU own the puck.
The players have separate lanes.

questions.prompt: What does this practice whistle mean?
questions.explanation: The briefing defines the signal for this activity.

questions.prompt: Which things help after that signal?
questions.explanation: Listening and awareness fit the instruction. These are suggested behaviours.

questions.prompt: Order this practice stop.
questions.explanation: The picture cannot measure stopping distance or technique.

questions.prompt: Is stopping the same as skating faster?
questions.explanation: Stopping and speeding up are different actions.

questions.prompt: Now the coach invites a restart in your lane. What could you do?

options.text: Check the lane and begin gently
Assume every whistle has the same meaning

questions.explanation: Follow the new instruction. Another activity may use different signals.

questions.prompt: Tell a grown-up what you would listen for next.
questions.explanation: The next instruction or permission to begin is relevant. An adult can record spoken words.

questions.prompt: You have stopped, but the puck slides away. What could YOU do while the coach is talking?

options.text: Listen and ask before going to get it
Ask Navy2 to race after it

questions.explanation: Stay with the stop-and-listen instruction. Ask for help collecting the puck rather than starting another chase.

questions.prompt: Before turning to listen, what helps YOU give Navy2 room?

options.text: Keep your stick in your own space

questions.explanation: Notice your partner while you turn and leave room for both players and their sticks.

questions.prompt: The coach asks Navy2 to use more space for the next try. Move Navy2 farther from YOUR lane.
questions.explanation: This separates the two practice lanes. It is a new coach-directed setup, not permission to restart before the next signal.

questions.prompt: You did not hear what the coach said next. What could you say?
questions.explanation: Try “Can you say that again?” or “Can you show me?” Asking helps you know when and where to start the next try.

scenarios.title: A teammate behind your shoulder
scenarios.objective: Look beyond the forward direction to find a teammate.
scenarios.briefing: YOU face the attacking end and hold the puck. Navy2 is behind your facing direction. Gold1 is ahead on the other side. The coach asks you to find Navy2 before deciding on a puck action. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU face +x.
Navy2 is behind that facing direction.
Finding Navy2 does not prove a pass is open.

questions.prompt: Where is Navy2 compared with the way YOU face?
questions.explanation: YOU face the attacking end while Navy2 is behind YOU.

questions.prompt: What can looking around help you find?
questions.explanation: Teammate locations and pressure are the source-supported information cues.

questions.prompt: Arrange this looking activity.

options.text: Tell the coach where Navy2 is

questions.explanation: This is the activity routine. A screen answer does not demonstrate a real shoulder check.

questions.prompt: For a second try, move YOU away from the side with Navy2.
questions.explanation: This changes the viewing relationship while leaving space. It is a practice reset, not an ideal game position.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 skates ahead of YOU. Should you keep pointing behind?
questions.explanation: Locate the teammate again when their position changes.

questions.prompt: Point to one thing you might miss by only watching the puck.
questions.explanation: Navy2 is a concrete example. A spoken answer or pointing is enough.

questions.prompt: Gold1 moves into the way ahead. What could YOU look for behind your shoulder?

options.text: Navy2 and a clear way to pass

questions.explanation: Navy2 is behind YOU. Looking there can reveal a different choice, but you still need a clear passing lane.

questions.prompt: What should YOU check before a pass back to Navy2?

options.text: Whether Gold1 can reach the passing lane
Only which way YOUR skates point

questions.explanation: A teammate behind you can help if you locate the target and check the lane. Facing forward does not remove the option of a pass back.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 to a new waiting place behind YOU, with room for a short pass.
questions.explanation: Navy2 stays behind the way YOU face and separate from YOUR spot. Several nearby places can give a different passing angle.

questions.prompt: Why might a short pass back to Navy2 help you go forward later?
questions.explanation: It can move the puck away from Gold1’s pressure and give your team another view of the space ahead. Passing back is useful when that lane is clear; you do not have to use it every time.

scenarios.title: Find the loose puck and a friend
scenarios.objective: Find a loose puck, notice pressure, and choose a nearby teammate after the pickup.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end and gold attacks the -x end. YOU are skating toward a loose puck in open ice. Navy2 is across the middle with room. Gold1 is approaching from the side nearest the boards. The coach asks you to look while you approach, then choose what helps.
cues: The puck is loose in open ice.
Navy2 is across the middle.
Gold1 approaches from the board side.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck now?
questions.explanation: The puck is loose, so nobody owns it yet. Find it before planning the next touch.

questions.prompt: What should you notice as you go to the puck?

options.text: Gold1 coming from the board side
Only the puck until it reaches your stick

questions.explanation: Keep finding the puck while checking Gold1 and Navy2. Their positions help you choose your first touch.

questions.prompt: Place YOU near the loose puck, with room to see Gold1.
questions.explanation: This spot brings YOU near the puck while leaving a little view of Gold1. It is one controlled approach example; another nearby spot can work.

questions.prompt: After reaching the loose puck, put these possible next events in order.

options.text: YOU send a pass toward Navy2

questions.explanation: This is one possible successful passing story, not a claim it already happened. Keep checking Gold1 during the approach and before the pass.

questions.prompt: Gold1 reaches the loose puck first and controls it. What should YOU change?

options.text: Read Gold1’s next move and help defend
Keep reaching for the puck as if it is loose
Continue the planned pass to Navy2

questions.explanation: Gold1 now has control, so YOU cannot carry or pass that puck. Keep watching and choose a useful defensive response with Navy2.

questions.prompt: Why does Navy2 matter after you find the puck?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is a navy teammate in open middle space. After you see the pressure, that space can give you a short passing choice if the lane stays clear.

scenarios.title: Find pressure before a corner pickup
scenarios.objective: Notice a loose puck, pressure and support before choosing a pickup route.
scenarios.briefing: A loose puck waits in the corner in the attacking end. YOU are nearest it. Gold1 is approaching from the inside of this practice area; Navy2 waits along the boards away from the corner. The approach is stated, not simulated. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The puck is loose in the corner.
Gold1 approaches from inside.
Navy2 offers a board-side partner.

questions.prompt: What is the puck's state at this freeze?
questions.explanation: No owner is assigned and the puck is near the corner.

questions.prompt: What could YOU find before the pickup?

options.text: The result of a pass that has not happened

questions.explanation: Locate pressure and support; do not assume a later result.

questions.prompt: You spotted Gold1 and Navy2 before moving. When should you look for them again?

options.text: Only once the puck is on your stick
Keep checking as you approach and before choosing your first touch
After you send the pass to Navy2

questions.explanation: Gold1 and Navy2 can move while you approach. Keep checking pressure and support along with the puck, so your first touch fits the newest picture. Looking once does not finish the job.

questions.prompt: Show a nearby approach point while keeping the pressure side in mind.
questions.explanation: This example approaches on the board side. It needs coaching and path checks; other angles may work.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 changes to the boards side. What must you update?
questions.explanation: A changed pressure side changes the information for the next decision.

questions.prompt: Why should finding the puck not be your only job here?
questions.explanation: The puck location alone does not reveal Gold1 or the partner option. This is a simple pickup read, not a structured breakout system.

questions.prompt: Navy2 sees Gold1 closing from the inside. What could Navy2 call to help YOU before the pickup?
questions.explanation: A short call such as “Pressure inside; I am along the boards” gives the pressure side and an outlet. YOU still checks the play: the call helps the scan and does not replace it.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 wins the puck before YOU, what could Navy2 do?

options.text: Check Gold1’s route and look for a useful passing lane to close
Look toward the Navy net and recover to help defend
Keep waiting in the old spot for a pass from YOU

questions.explanation: Gold1 now has possession, so Navy2’s job changes from offering an outlet to helping defend. Recovering or closing an available lane can help; if Navy2 can reach the puck under control, challenging it may also fit.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 to offer a shorter pass along the boards once YOU gain control.
questions.explanation: The example brings Navy2 closer along the board side while staying away from Gold1’s inside approach. A shorter outlet can help after the pickup, but Navy2 must keep checking whether Gold1 can close the lane.

questions.prompt: The puck is near where the side boards curve around the end of the rink. What do we call this area?
questions.explanation: This is the corner. The slot is the middle space in front of the net; the point is near the attacking blue line. Naming the corner helps a teammate understand where the pickup is happening.

scenarios.title: Face the play while moving back
scenarios.objective: Connect stated backward movement with seeing the approaching play.
scenarios.briefing: The coach says YOU are practising moving backward toward the defending end while facing the attacking end. The picture is a freeze, not a moving trace. Gold1 carries the puck toward YOU; Navy2 waits behind and to one side. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU face the attacking end.
The stated exercise moves YOU toward the defending end.
Gold1 is ahead of the facing direction.

questions.prompt: Which way does the coach say YOU are moving?
questions.explanation: This comes from the stated exercise. The static picture does not independently show velocity.

questions.prompt: Which player is ahead of the way YOU face?
questions.explanation: Gold1 is ahead of YOU, in the direction YOU face.

questions.prompt: What can this exercise ask you to notice?
questions.explanation: You can discuss the visible play. The display does not measure physical skating.

questions.prompt: Show another practice position a little farther back while facing the play.
questions.explanation: This matches the stated movement direction. It is not a universal defensive gap or proof that the skate is feasible.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 changes direction. What could you do before another movement?

options.text: Keep moving because the first plan never changes

questions.explanation: Update the cue. The correct physical transition needs on-ice instruction and a validated trace.

questions.prompt: What is different about facing a direction and moving in that direction?
questions.explanation: A player can face the play while moving backward. Use the stated exercise rather than guessing motion from a still image.

questions.prompt: Gold1 gets too close for comfortable backward movement. What could help in this practice?

options.text: Turn and skate to regain room while checking Gold1
Stay backward even if Gold1 goes past
Reach with the stick and stop moving

questions.explanation: A controlled turn can help regain room. The coach should teach and observe that movement on ice; there is no fixed gap that fits every skater.

questions.prompt: What should YOU check when turning to move back faster?

options.text: Where Gold1 and the puck are going
Whether the route behind is clear of Navy2
Only how quickly YOU can turn

questions.explanation: Keep track of the carrier and the space you are moving into. Speed alone does not tell you whether the route is useful or clear.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 to a waiting spot behind YOU that leaves the straight retreat lane clear.
questions.explanation: This keeps Navy2 to one side of YOUR path toward the defending end. The actual skating route still depends on how Gold1 moves.

questions.prompt: How could Navy2 help YOU notice space behind without taking over your looking?
questions.explanation: Navy2 can give a short call about their location or a clear route. YOU still checks while moving; a call adds information and does not replace looking.

scenarios.title: The blocked pass is loose
scenarios.objective: Distinguish a pass attempt from completed reception.
scenarios.briefing: A pass from Navy2 was deflected and now lies loose between the players. This picture begins after the deflection; no path is animated. YOU have not collected it yet. Gold1 is nearby and Navy2 remains available. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The pass did not reach a controlled receiver.
The puck has no owner.
Both teams can see the loose puck.

questions.prompt: Did the pass finish with YOU controlling it?
questions.explanation: The briefing and setup identify a loose puck, not a completed reception.

questions.prompt: Which facts are present now?

options.text: YOU already made the next shot

questions.explanation: A loose puck and a nearby opponent are shown; a next shot is not.

questions.prompt: Order the supplied puck events.

options.text: It is loose at this freeze

questions.explanation: This is declared history. The earlier path is not simulated.

questions.prompt: Show a nearby place from which YOU could approach the loose puck.
questions.explanation: This moves toward the puck without claiming who will reach it first. Check other players before a real approach.

questions.prompt: Imagine Gold1 controls it first. Which plan needs to change?

options.text: A plan to shoot it yourself immediately

questions.explanation: YOU cannot perform a puck action while Gold1 controls it. Update possession before choosing.

questions.prompt: Why is attempted pass different from completed pass?
questions.explanation: A pass can be deflected or stay loose. Control by the receiver must actually happen.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 controls the loose puck first, which responses could help Navy defend?

options.text: Protect a useful route toward the navy net
Keep waiting in the old passing spot
Find Navy2 so you can cover different space

questions.explanation: Possession has changed. Read Gold1 and the route to your net, then use Navy2’s location to avoid both chasing the same space.

questions.prompt: Which statements does the briefing actually tell us?

options.text: YOU have not collected the puck

questions.explanation: The deflection and lack of a controlled reception are stated. The briefing does not say who touched the pass.

questions.prompt: Place YOU on the navy-net side of the loose puck, with room to approach.
questions.explanation: This keeps YOU nearer the navy end than the loose puck while changing the approach angle. Check Gold1 and Gold2; it does not guarantee who wins the puck.

questions.prompt: After YOU collect it, why might a pass back to Navy2 help against Gold2 ahead?
questions.explanation: Navy2 offers support behind YOU, away from Gold2’s side. If the lane is clear, a pass back can keep possession and create a new angle. Check Gold1 too before using it.

scenarios.title: Our half-ice change signal
scenarios.objective: Recognize the puck-release and change routine in a named game model.
scenarios.briefing: This activity uses the Hockey Canada U9 half-ice change rule: on the designated change signal, release the puck and leave for the next unit while play continues. The signal has just sounded while YOU control the puck. The full-rink picture shows player relationships only, not the exact half-ice layout or bench. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The designated change signal was stated.
YOU still own the puck at this instant.
The next unit waits off the illustrated area.

questions.prompt: Who must release the puck at this instant?

options.text: Gold1, who does not have it

questions.explanation: YOU are the declared puck owner when the change signal sounds.

questions.prompt: Which instructions belong to this named routine?

options.text: Finish a long attack before changing

questions.explanation: Those actions follow the quoted model in the briefing. Local program applicability still needs review.

questions.prompt: Arrange the declared change sequence.

options.text: The next unit continues the activity

questions.explanation: This describes the model, not a moving trace or a universal rule for all games.

questions.prompt: Does the whole game stop for this stated change?
questions.explanation: The briefing states that play continues under this half-ice model.

questions.prompt: Imagine a different practice says whistle means stop and listen. Which instruction applies there?
questions.explanation: Signals need context. A practice stop and this game change routine are different.

questions.prompt: How can you know which whistle routine the coach is using?
questions.explanation: Listen to the activity instructions and ask if unclear. The scenario does not establish a rule for every U9 program.

questions.prompt: After YOU release the puck, Gold1 reaches it. In this change routine, what should YOU do?

options.text: Continue leaving for the next unit
Chase Gold1 to win it back first
Stay until Navy2 gets the puck

questions.explanation: The designated signal still means release and change in this named activity. A new puck owner does not cancel the change instruction.

questions.prompt: What helps the next unit take its turn in this activity?

options.text: Release the puck when the change signal sounds
Leave using the route the coach explained
Take the puck with YOU to the waiting players

questions.explanation: Release control and make room for the next unit. Use the real activity’s exit route; the picture does not show the bench.

questions.prompt: This picture does not show the waiting area. How should YOU find the exit route for your real game?

options.text: Use the route the coach explained; ask if unclear
Head for whichever boards look closest

questions.explanation: The coach or official can show the actual change route. Do not invent an exit from a picture that only shows player relationships.

questions.prompt: Why should YOU leave after the signal even when the attacking end is nearby?
questions.explanation: In this named half-ice routine, the signal gives the next unit its turn while play continues. Being near the attacking end does not mean finishing another attack first. Other game formats can use different routines.

scenarios.title: Make room after the goalie whistle
scenarios.objective: Recognize possession and space after a scoped goalie-freeze restart.
scenarios.briefing: In the named Hockey Canada U9 half-ice model, a goalie-freeze whistle gives the defending team possession and asks attackers to retreat. The gold goalie already held the puck and the whistle happened. Gold1 now controls the restart puck near the crease; YOU are a navy attacker asked to back away. Earlier events are stated, not animated. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The goalie freeze and whistle already happened.
Gold1 now has restart possession.
The crease is near the gold goal.

questions.prompt: Who controls the restart puck in the current picture?

options.text: The gold goalie still holds it

questions.explanation: The current owner is Gold1. The goalie's earlier hold is part of the supplied history.

questions.prompt: What named area is beside this restart?

options.text: The crease by the gold net

questions.explanation: Gold1 is near the gold goal at the +x end and its crease; this is a rink landmark, not a new crease-entry rule.

questions.prompt: Order the stated restart events.
questions.explanation: These events are given by the briefing and need not be inferred from a static image.

questions.prompt: Move YOU away to give the restarting team room.
questions.explanation: This reference creates more separation. The official directs the exact retreat in the real model; this point is not a certified distance test.

questions.prompt: What should YOU pay attention to before resuming?

options.text: An automatic faceoff after every hold

questions.explanation: Follow the named model and the actual signal rather than importing another game's restart.

questions.prompt: Why do you need to give Gold1 room before play continues?
questions.explanation: In this named Hockey Canada U9 half-ice model, attackers back off three metres after the goalie freezes the puck. That gives the defending team room to restart with possession. Follow the instructions for your local game format; do not assume every North American U9 program uses this restart.

questions.prompt: Gold1 starts moving with the restart puck while YOU are still backing away. What guides YOUR next action?

options.text: The official’s restart instruction for this activity
Whether Gold1 looks close enough to challenge

questions.explanation: Follow the named restart instruction and complete the required retreat. Another player moving does not by itself establish that YOU may challenge.

questions.prompt: During the retreat, what should YOU keep track of?

options.text: Navy2’s space so you do not both crowd the same route
The old shooting lane as if the whistle never happened

questions.explanation: Keep the new possession and your teammate in view while giving the restarting team room. The earlier shooting chance has ended.

questions.prompt: Place YOU a little away from the crease area with the puck side visible.
questions.explanation: This example gives YOU room after the named whistle while keeping the puck side in view. The coach's setup still controls the next move.

questions.prompt: Why should a whistle make you reset your read?
questions.explanation: The puck may be in a new place and a different player may control the next action. Resetting prevents carrying an old plan into a changed activity.
